panels.figure_caption: The female patient with Patau syndrome as an infant presenting phenotypic changes in Trisomy 13, including cleft lip, trigger thumbs and rocker bottom feet.
in_text_mentions: ion, the patient exhibited several phenotypic features consistent with Patau syndrome, including cleft lip and palate, ocular hypertelorism, low-set ears, low anterior hairline, cutis aplasia, microcephaly, overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet (Figure 1). No pulmonary, genital, renal abnormalities, or polydactyly were identified. Congenital heart defects, including ventricular septal defect (VSD), atrial septal defect (ASD), patent foramen ovale (PFO), and bicuspid aortic valve were identified; however, the girl remained hemodynamically stable and did not require cardiovascular support.

plate_findings.evidence: absence of scalp and calvarium in the parietal region

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left image is coronal T2 head MRI from trisomy 13 newborn (9th day of life, female karyotype with three copies of chromosome 13). Caption explicitly states absence of scalp and calvarium in parietal region with no herniation, matching patau_syndrome_cutis_aplasia vocabulary (aplasia cutis congenita / parieto-occipital scalp defect). B: Right image is sagittal T1 head MRI from same trisomy 13 newborn. Caption states absence of scalp and calvarium in parietal region with no herniation, matching patau_syndrome_cutis_aplasia.
panels.attribution_text: AlMatrafi et al. Case report: Aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp with bone defect and an exposed sagittal sinus in a trisomy 13 newborn.. Frontiers in pediatrics 2023. doi:10.3389/fped.2023.1142950. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

in_text_mentions: including the TORCH test (toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus), was negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody were non-reactive and the core antibody was negative. The blood culture did not show bacterial growth. On the 9th day of life, chromosomal analysis showed a female karyotype with three copies of chromosome number 13 (trisomy 13) in all 20 metaphase cell counts. Radiology investigations included head magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and revealed absence of scalp and calvarium at the parietal region with no herniation visualized, as shown in Figure 2.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A captioned as cardiac alteration in Patau syndrome: calcification in mitral valve chordae (golf ball). Fetal obstetric ultrasound patient image. No vocabulary finding_key covers isolated chordal calcification, captured as proposed findings. in_text_mentions: hypoplasia, low implantation of the ears, bilateral incisive transforaminal cleft lip and palate 7 (Figure 2A), hypotelorism with increased lens density (Figure 2B), bilateral polydactyly (Figure 3) of hands and feet, presence of golf-ball sign (calcification of the mitral valve chordae) (Figure 4A), and hypoplasia of left heart chambers, especially ventricular (Figure 4B). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a newborn's scalp showing a large full-thickness cutis aplasia defect with exposed brain tissue and sagittal sinus. The article title and in-text explicitly attribute this to trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), and parieto-occipital cutis aplasia is a recognized classic feature of trisomy 13. B: Second clinical photograph of the same newborn's scalp defect from a different angle, showing the full-thickness cutis aplasia with exposed brain tissue and sagittal sinus. The article title and in-text explicitly attribute this to trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), and parieto-occipital cutis aplasia is a recognized classic feature of trisomy 13.
